speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to move the adjournment of the house -

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN ASKING LEAVE TO MOVE ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Order. If the hon. member is making a motion to adjourn the house under standing order 31, this is not the proper time to do so. Standing order 31 reads as follows:
Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (standing order 15) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
The question of the proper time at which to make this motion was discussed briefly in the house on November 7, 1949. At that time I pointed out that in my opinion the proper time to make this motion was immediately before notices of motions or orders of the day. I have considered the matter since that time and am of the opinion that if it had been the intention of parliament when this rule was introduced that the motion should be made immediately after routine proceedings, the rule would have stopped there; that is to say, it would have read:
Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business.
But the rule parliament approved went further and added:
-and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
It is clear that the motion is made after the daily routine of business. In my opinion it is equally clear that it should be made immediately before notices of motions or orders of the day. I believe that the reason why the rule was drawn in this way was to make sure that all the business of the house which was not of a controversial nature would be duly attended to. Hon. members know that in the daily routine of business there is little that is debatable. Under questions, there is nothing that is debatable. Again, under notices of motions for the production of papers, there is nothing that is debatable. That is the kind of business that must be disposed of. I therefore rule that the motion to adjourn the house under standing order 31 must be made after the ordinary daily routine of business has been concluded and immediately before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave,
seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the announcement yesterday of the greatest monthly increase in Canadian cost of living during the month of February to the disastrously high level of 179-7 points; and the urgent need for vigorous action by the government and the immediate adoption of such measures as will halt inflation, hold down the cost of living and restore confidence in the Canadian dollar.

It is my duty to decide whether this motion is in order and also whether it is of urgent public importance. The meaning of urgency as set forth in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 174, is as follows:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate," when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough . . .
Today being Thursday there can be no debate upon going into supply. Under standing order 28, when such an order is called on a Thursday or Friday, the Speaker leaves the chair without question put. If I thought there would1 be in the immediate future an opportunity to debate this matter, I would not consider it to be urgent within the meaning of the rules. However, I do not at the present time see that there will be an opportunity for discussing this matter in the immediate future.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the budget is being brought down next Tuesday and that a debate of this kind is of course appropriate under the budget. As to urgency, the figures referred to were with regard to the increase in the cost of living during the month of February, which is some five weeks

ago. The fact that they were published only a day or two ago does not, I think, suggest that we should urgently deal with a matter that happened five weeks ago.
I would also point out that the matter of the increase in the cost of living has been discussed on two occasions during this session. Therefore it seems to me that the motion is out of order.

Mr. Speaker, as I have introduced the motion and as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has expressed his view, I would ask your permission to offer my reasons for believing that this matter should be debated at this time. Under the practice of this house, there will not be an opportunity either today, tomorrow or on Monday to introduce a motion which would make it possible-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Monday, if we move to go into supply, that will certainly be an opportune time to discuss any matter or any grievance against the government.
Did you say "if"?

The Minister of Public Works
(Mr. Fournier) has indicated uncertainty with regard to Monday or Tuesday by the use of the word "if" which he has introduced into his remarks; because it is possible for the house to proceed to deal with the estimates of the departments already introduced without introducing a new motion to go into supply. Therfore there is no assurance that the house will be able to deal with this subject.
As to the question of urgency raised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the fact that the figures published yesterday related to accumulated figures of five weeks ago, what he says is perfectly true. But this is the first occasion on which the house has had an opportunity to express its opinion with regard to such an important indication of the trend which affects every Canadian. I suggest that there is no single subject having regard to the domestic affairs of Canada today which so urgently calls for consideration by this house, and there is no subject upon which the members of this house should have an opportunity at an earlier date to express their opinion than upon this runaway inflation that is now evidenced by these figures that we have seen.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the motion before you seeks the opportunity for the members of this house to indicate at the earliest possible moment their own belief as to whether or not the situation disclosed by

these figures, and the trend which they make apparent, should be dealt with in some way by the government at this time. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you with respect that if there is any question on this point you permit the members of this house to decide by their recorded vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say just a word on the question of urgency, Mr. Speaker? As the house knows, on Tuesday evening I intend to move that the house go into committee of ways and means. In the course of my remarks preceding that motion I shall have a good deal to say on this world-wide phenomenon of inflation-it is not confined to Canada-and every hon. member will have an opportunity of voicing his views before the motion is put to the house.
I suggest that the question of urgency, which of course is for Your Honour to decide, is not such as to necessitate two debates on . the same subject, on which we have already had two in this house, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has indicated.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-
The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar has the floor.

I should like to support the view expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). We intended to introduce a motion in terms almost identical with that suggested by the leader of the opposition. I should like to point this out. While it is perfectly true that the budget will be brought down on Tuesday evening, yet the debate on the budget is not a narrow one. We debate all matters regarding the Canadian economy and the Canadian financial system, taxation and all the rest of it. I submit that this is a matter of some urgency, Mr. Speaker.
It is true that the figures produced yesterday relate to a situation that developed some weeks ago, but since then we have had more of this runaway inflation and the house should be given an opportunity to discuss the matter now in order that the government may know now, before the vote on the budget is taken or the discussion on the budget has taken place, what the opinion of this house is in that connection.
And I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter of some urgency affecting the welfare of great masses of the Canadian people. Indeed, I heard over the radio yesterday that in one of our Canadian cities people living on fixed incomes, old age pensions and the like, are suffering from malnutrition. This house has no right to delay the discussion on

this subject when people of this country are suffering from malnutrition because of the runaway inflation.
On a point of order-
Order.
On a point of order-

to the hon. member for Springfield that it is irregular to raise a point of order on a point of order. However, it may be that the hon. member for Springfield is raising the question as to whether or not this matter is urgent. I will hear the hon. member for Springfield.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of
order, there are others in this house who are interested in what is going on in this country besides the leader of the opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party. I quite agree with you when you rule that the-

Order. I have made no
such ruling as the hon. member has suggested. I will hear the Minister of Public Works, unless the hon. member for Springfield wishes to state his point of order briefly.

Mr. Speaker, my point of
order is this. According to Beauchesne's parliamentary rules and forms, third edition, 1943:

My point of order is this. I do not wish to discuss anything which has already been discussed in the session. I merely wish to discuss the rising-
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that your ruling will have to conform to citation 174 of Beauchesne, third edition, which reads:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate," when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
Our difficulty in discussing this citation is that the decision and the ruling will be in your discretion, even though the leader of the opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party will tell us that if we do not discuss this question immediately a catastrophe will occur in the country. It is so important that we should hear their voices right now, but if we

Cost of Living
do not hear their voices a calamity will take place in our country. That may be true. They believe that. They think that if they do not speak in this house today it will be too late for the salvation of the country. Well, if you agree with these two hon. gentlemen, any hon. member who is convinced that what is going on in the country is not right could use that same argument. And it has been, used twice in this session with as much force and in as violent language by certain members of the opposition whom I have heard in the house. They have said, if we do not discuss the high cost of living, if we do not impose controls immediately our country will be out of luck. Now, Mr. Speaker will, in his mind-and I am trying to be fair-have to decide if it is so important that members of the opposition, or even members on the government side, have to tell us that the cost of living has gone up 4 points plus something. Everybody in the country knows that.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said: We have to tell the house and the country what is taking place. Well, they just learned it from the papers yesterday.
Mr. Speaker,-
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may we have a few minutes? I cannot come back at eight o'clock and argue the matter.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that the motion was not presented with the explanation that it was for the purpose of telling the government that their own figures were accurate. This is not so hilarious a subject as some hon. members seem to think. The purpose of the motion is to permit hon. members to say in this house that they think action should be taken now to deal with the situation disclosed by the figures.
Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman has something to add to what the leader of the opposition has said.
May I say-

-it is true I read in the newspapers what the hon, gentleman says. But if the government knew this before, then they have been derelict in their duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You see, it may have been urgent that the hon. member say that to the government right now. But we learned this, as the public learned it, when figures were brought out by the statistics branch.
[Mr. Fournier (Hull).J
Now, my fear is that even after listening to what you gentlemen will say, it will not change the minds of the people.
The government.
We want to change the mind of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am speaking of the people we represent in this house. It would not change the minds of the people, because they have read the same thing you have read in the papers.
That does not follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You want to amplify in debate what you already saw in the press. I do not believe you have the right to do it; I think you are wrong in trying to do it. The question, Mr. Speaker, is if it is in your opinion for the good of the people of Canada that this evening we should-
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are the only one who believes it. Is it your opinion that we should listen to these gentlemen during the evening, and that it will change the situation so that it will force the government tomorrow, which is Friday-we cannot do it on Saturday-
Does not the government act on Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -to introduce legislation which would not be carried tomorrow? Is it your opinion that this will help the situation in Canada? I do not know that it will.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is legislation now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Even if we have, it is not by the speeches that you make that the government would take a decision it did not wish to take.
And, Mr. Speaker, after listening to the eloquent speeches these gentlemen will make, there will be no immediate change in the country. I suggest that on Monday, as a first order, I move that we go into supply. That is only Monday. At that time we could discuss the whole situation. We will have the whole thing before us to make a decision. However, if you try it before, I am not sure you will impress the members of the government, who have to attend certain functions, with which the opposition told us they were ready to help us.
We have taken these engagements. Probably I will have to sit here at eight o'clock and argue the whole thing out, because my colleagues want to attend the function. And immediately after you have made those speeches, the result will be the same. There

will be no change, even in the minds of the people because I do not think you are convincing enough to make the people change their minds. And when you are through at eleven o'clock the subject will have been-
Horsed around.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, the subject will have been spent, and the result will be more speeches on Hansard concerning the cost of living, speeches that could be made on Monday just as well.
I would ask the leader of the opposition in his kindly way to withdraw this motion.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
He would have the support of his colleagues if he were to do so, I suppose. I would ask that he withdraw this motion, and on Monday I will move to go into supply, when that subject may be considered.
If that is satisfactory, then Mr. Speaker would not have to make a ruling, which would be quite embarrassing because it might mean he does not believe that speeches by certain members are so urgent.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the request made I would point out that having regard to the subject I have raised I do not propose to withdraw the motion. I would suggest that in view of the fact that the Minister of Public Works has indicated that there are other matters of importance, the house might well agree in the belief that the minister perhaps is not exactly correct, and that you should make your ruling in regard to the motion.

Mr. Speaker, this is a matter you will have to take the responsibility of deciding. I have listened to many discussions on points of order in this house in regard to this standing order, but I certainly have never heard anything suggested such as the Minister of Public Works has suggested today. Surely it has not reached the point where an opposition or a private member cannot make a motion of this kind, and cannot ask the government to act. Surely that is no reason for refusing the motion. That does not say that an emergency does not exist.
The motion we are discussing now is not on the general question of the cost of living, but rather a proposal to discuss the enormous increase in the cost of living announced yesterday, and the effect that will have on the people of Canada. And, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you that a question that is of great urgency, such as this one, cannot be left over
Cost of Living
until some convenient time when we could discuss it. Because if it could be left over it is no longer a question of urgency.
May I draw the attention of the house to standing order 31 (3), which says that the member moving the motion-
-then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house. If objection is taken, Mr. Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and, if more than twenty members rise accordingly, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.
Now, sir, the point is clear, that if in your opinion the question before us is not one of urgent public importance you will say so, and that ends it; but if you believe it is a question of urgent public importance you will ascertain the wish of the members of the house, and they will decide whether or not the question will be discussed.
Order; I will hear the hon. member for Glengarry.

As a producer of eggs, I am bewildered by this motion, because during the last war there was a ceiling of fifty cents a dozen on eggs, and I was receiving fifty cents a dozen during that time. I was home during Easter week, and we were receiving only forty-eight cents a dozen. If that is an increase in the cost of living, I cannot see it.

I am placed in a rather difficult position, but I must make a ruling, in accordance with the established procedure in the house.
It was mentioned by one hon. member that there had been a previous debate on this subject, and that is correct. When a motion similar to this one was made shortly after that debate I raised the question as to whether it was in order. However, some considerable time has intervened, and I would not at this time rule the motion out of order merely because there had been a previous debate some time ago on a subject relating to the increase in the cost of living.
By not ruling the motion out of order on that ground I would not want it to be taken as a precedent so that every time there is a rise in the cost of living a motion like this would be considered in order. This matter is of some importance because the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has moved a motion, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has attempted to move a motion and the hon. member for Springfield has also attempted to move a motion. Accordingly it is a very important matter, and I think we all agree that that is so.

Cost of Living
It was suggested that the budget will be brought down on Tuesday night after which time there will be an opportunity to discuss this question. I must however point out to the house that it is customary after the budget is brought down to adjourn the debate thereon for several days, sometimes for a week, in order that hon. members may familiarize themselves with the contents of the budget. So there is no assurance that hon. members will be given an opportunity to speak on this subject in the immediate future.
I may say that until the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) spoke I was firmly of the opinion that this motion came within the rules of urgency as set forth in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 174. The question is not how urgent the matter is so far as you and I and all the people of Canada are concerned, but how urgent it is having regard to the opportunity which will be given to hon. members of this house to debate the subject. If the Minister of Public Works had not risen and said that at the opening of the house on Monday he would move to go into committee of supply I would have ruled that this matter was one which was urgent within the rules of the house.
However, the Minister of Public Works, speaking on behalf of the government, has stated that on Monday he will move a motion to go into committee of supply as the first order of business. I might point out to hon. members that if I declared that this motion was one of urgency within the rules of the house the debate could go on just for the three hours this evening and that would be the end. After that time hon. members would not have an opportunity to discuss the matter because standing order 31 provides that such a motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session. That is to say, either tomorrow or on Monday an hon. member could not move the adjournment of the house for this purpose.
When the Minister of Public Works moves that the house go into committee of supply on Monday there will be at least six hours during which hon. members can discuss this matter. Added to that an hon. member will be able to move a motion with respect to the matter. At the present time an hon. member could not move such a motion. Since the Minister of Public Works, speaking for the government, has stated that he will move that the house go into supply on Monday I rule that this question is not one of urgency today. Hon. members will have an opportunity to discuss this matter on Monday in accordance with the assurance given by the Minister of Public Works.

Mr. Speaker, with the reason that has been given for not permitting a debate now, and without accepting that as having the finality that there would be if a vote were called, I simply would explain that I do not propose to ask for a vote on the ruling in view of what has been said about the debate on Monday. But I do give notice to you that I shall introduce an amendment at the time the motion is made to go into committee of supply.

Introduce your same motion.

speechtext:

471. Departmental administration, $1,199,818.
Is the minister making a statement on this?
On what?
Is the minister making a statement?
I do not propose to make a statement. I propose to proceed in the usual manner, and if hon. members have certain matters they wish to raise I shall try to deal with them as well as I can.

Mr. Chairman, it is quite
evident that we are going to have a quiet homey evenings with only the best of us here. I should get unanimous support for that remark.
Including the best minister.

However, I know that the other ministers and members are busy with very important duties helping to entertain the President of France. This is the first occasion on which the estimates of the Department of Transport for the present fiscal year have
Supply-Transport
been under consideration. Before proceeding to deal with the department, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on his appointment as parliamentary assistant to the minister. He has been a very conscientious member, and I am quite sure will fill this post with great benefit to the country and great honour to himself. I wish him good luck.
This year the most important business to be considered by the house under the estimates of the Department of Transport is the report of the royal commission on transportation. The whole problem of transportation has always been one of the main questions facing Canadian legislatures and the Canadian people. That is perfectly understandable of course because of the vast distances in this country and the scattered settlements from one coast to the other. There probably would have been no Canada as we know it today if special provision had not been made to link the maritimes with what was known as Upper Canada by the Intercolonial Railway, and also to link British Columbia with central Canada by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Today, just as in the days following confederation, transportation is of vital importance to the Canadian people. We are fortunate at this session in having had a report from the royal commission on transportation. The commissioners have gone into most of the aspects of our transportation problem, and I think have made a very important report. Whether or not one agrees with all the recommendations, the fact remains that the men who made this investigation are very distinguished Canadians, the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, who was chairman, Dr. H. F. Angus of British Columbia and Dr. H. A. Innis of Toronto. They brought to their work a great zeal to serve their country and displayed ability in conducting this investigation; I think this is one of the most important reports ever to have been placed before the Canadian parliament.
We have not had the report very long. It was tabled a few days before the house recessed for Easter, and probably very few members have had the opportunity to study it carefully. It is a lengthy report, and I must admit that I personally have not reviewed it as carefully as I propose to do. I hope the house will be given an opportunity to study it thoroughly, and for this purpose it might be possible to make use of one of the committees of the house. We have a very competent committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; I cannot say anything else, because I am a member of that committee. I see no reason why that committee could not

Supply-Transport
make a study of this report. From what the Prime Minister said when he tabled it, I take it some legislation will be placed before the house, and in any event I urge the minister to refer that legislation to this committee. In that way it will be possible to have such legislation given more careful consideration than if it goes through the house here in the ordinary way; it would also enable members of the committee to get a better understanding of at least some of Canada's transportation problems.
That is important, because from this report we have an opportunity to work out a national policy on transportation. Of course there would be differences of opinion on different aspects of such a policy, but it might be surprising how close to unanimity we could come on such a policy. You see, Mr. Chairman, transportation does not involve only the railways. It includes shipping, under which we have ocean-going shipping, coastal shipping, the traffic on the great lakes and the shipping through the canals, which is increasing in importance all the time and will continue to do so, particularly if the St. Lawrence seaway should be constructed. We have the airways, steadily becoming more important in Canada. They have been important from the start of flying and Canada has made great progress in aviation. Young Canadians seem to take to the air naturally; they make wonderful fliers. Aviation in our north country has always been far ahead of similar flying in any other country, and aviation generally is of great importance to our people.
Then some of the members have heard of pipe lines, which have become another aspect of the transportation problem facing this country. They would be included in a study such as I have' mentioned.
Then there are the highways. There is quite an insistent demand that the federal government should step into the highway picture. I am not taking sides on that question tonight, and merely say that the commission expressed doubt as to just how far the dominion government could go in the matter of regulating highway traffic. In any event, the highways do enter into the transportation picture.
So here we have a series of recommendations which might very well be worked into a good transportation policy for Canada. It would be a great tragedy if we allowed this report to be treated as parliament treated the Rowell-Sirois report. That was a splendid report prepared after a great deal of work by exceptionally capable men. I believe Dr. Angus was also a member of that commission. Parliament did not have an opportunity to

debate that report. I always thought it was a great tragedy that we did not thoroughly discuss and study the Rowell-Sirois report. I am sure that if we had done so there would have been beneficial results to Canada. Let us not have the same thing happen to this Turgeon report on transportation.
This evening I have no intention of going into the various recommendations at any length, but I would ask the minister to deal with at least some of the matters covered in the report. For instance, there is a very interesting proposal at page 253 in a chapter entitled "The rail link between east and west." It describes northern Ontario, the territory from Fort William to Sudbury, as a land bridge between eastern and western Canada, where practically no freight or passenger traffic originates. The commission finds this to be a sort of no man's land, and recommends that the government of Canada pay a subsidy to the railways to cover the cost of operating in that area. At page 253 of the report there is a very good summary of the attitude of the commission on this point:
The overhead cost of linking east and west together has been a matter of national concern from the earliest days. It is the existence of this necessary link between Canada's two vast areas that must be recognized. It is called for, not only by the requirements of the exchange of goods for commercial purposes, but also by those of our national defence structure. The problem presented is that of maintaining this link so long at least as it does not provide sufficient revenue for its own maintenance. This problem concerns the whole country and not only its western portion, and the responsibility for its solution should be assumed by the nation as, for instance, in the case of the maintenance of our canal system.
As hon. members know, the canal system, which is largely in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, is maintained by the country without cost to the users of those canals. Then the commissioners, after referring to this link as a bridge, go on to recommend-
. . . with the whole cost of maintaining the bridge over which the traffic between the two large areas must pass, just as the toll-free canals in central Canada are maintained at public expense for the passage of traffic through them.
The report states that the estimated amount of subsidy would be about $7 million annually. Those of us who come through that part of the country several times a year realize how accurate the picture is that is painted by the commissioners. I believe they have made out a splendid case for subsidization of this particular traffic. I hope that the government will accept that recommendation and will provide a subsidy during the present session. ^ I would ask that the minister deal with this recommendation when he replies.
Another recommendation on which I should like to have his remarks is contained

at page 122 of the report in a chapter entitled "Equalization". This chapter sets out that it now appears to be fairly generally accepted by the government and also by the railways that there should be a broad principle of equalization of rates throughout the country. The commissioners point out that in April of 1948 order in council P.C. 1487 was passed, which directed the board of transport commissioners to conduct a freight rate investigation-
. . . with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities . . .
That was an order in council passed of course by the present government in April of 1948. The railways apparently have not quarrelled very violently with the suggestion that there should be a broad general principle of equalization of these rates. One suggestion that the commissioners make is that on the long hauls the rates should be based on greater distance than on the short hauls. To make myself clear, let me put it this way. For example, if it costs $100 to move freight one hundred miles on a short haul, on the long haul that charge should be $100 for two hundred miles. I think that explains one of the suggestions they had in mind, namely, that the rate should not be just on a basis of mile for mile, but where a long haul was involved, should be lower than where there was a short haul.
They say the objective should be to get a uniform rate structure. At page 127, paragraph 10, we find this statement. They have listed various items which could help to bring about this result and say:
The foregoing items point to a new departure in class rates and commodity mileage rates, and eventually, in so far as practicable, in special or specific rates for the Canadian portion of the North American continent. It appears that Canada has reached a stage in its development when former methods of making regional rates must give way to a uniform rate structure that, as far as may be possible, will treat all citizens, localities, districts and1 regions alike.
That of course has been the plea of seven of the provinces of Canada for many years; it has been the plea of all of the provinces except Ontario and Quebec which seem to be satisfied with the present rate structure. One can understand that, because in Ontario and Quebec there is competition by road and by water to a far greater extent than there is in any of the other seven provinces. The result is that the rates in Ontario and Quebec are not as high as they are in the other provinces, and certainly not as high as they are in western Canada. I am not mentioning the position in Newfoundland because I am
Supply-Transport
not fully informed on that particular aspect of the subject. One reason I am pointing out this question of equalization to the minister is that the commission recommends that there be legislation. This improvement can only be made by an amendment to the Railway Act. In paragraph 12 on page 127 the commissioners recommend1 as follows:
Changes should be made in the "traffic, tolls and tariffs" sections of the Railway Act in order to empower the board to effect and maintain the uniformity in rates throughout Canada herein recommended.
If the government accepts that recommendation-and I hope it will-then let legislation be brought in at this session so that a start can be made on complying with the recommendation of the commission.
Another subject which is also of great importance and which likewise calls for an amendment to the Railway Act is that of transcontinental rates. They are dealt with at page 96 of the report, and I refer particularly to page 101 where it is stated:
The Railway Act should be amended to provide that when the competitive transcontinental tariffs are published by the railways, such tariffs shall contain a provision that the rates to or from intermediate territory shall not exceed the transcontinental rates by more than one-third.
As I understand it, the meaning of that recommendation is this. There are certain special transcontinental rates, for example, from Toronto and Montreal to Vancouver. They are only in effect because there is competition by sea and we benefit by those rates on the west coast. I presume there is also a similar benefit from transcontinental rates on the east coast. But the Canadians who live in the interior part of the country-for example, in interior British Columbia, in Alberta and, I suppose, in Saskatchewan as well-do not get any benefits from those transcontinental rates. They must pay a much higher rate. The commission has recommended that the higher rate that they pay in the interior portions of the country shall not be more than one-third higher than the transcontinental rates. I believe that that provision, if it became law, would be of great benefit to those Canadians who are not privileged to live at the seashore. I hope that the government will bring in an amendment to the Railway Act at this session to make that change possible as well.
Then there are in the report sections dealing with three subjects which I shall link together. First of all, there is the subject of Crowsnest pass rates. The reference to those rates will be found beginning at page 238. As hon. members know, those are the rates which enable wheat to be shipped to either coast at a freight

Supply-Transport
rate lower than the ordinary one. The finding of the commissioners is that there should be no change in those Crows-nest rates.
Then there are the provisions under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The report on these provisions is found at page 228, and there is a recommendation that there should be no change, that the benefits under the Maritime Freight Rates Act should not be cut down. They do recommend that there be some amendments to the act to bring it into line with the actual practice in the administration of the act.
The third subject which I wish to link with the other two is the question of amalgamation or unification of the railways. We find at pages 128 and 276 a very definite recommendation by the commission that there should be no unification of the railways and no amalgamation. I would like to know from the minister this evening the intention of the government on these three points:	whether
or not the recommendations of the commission on the Crowsnest rates, the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the question of amalgamation will be accepted. I may say that personally the recommendations seem to me to be very sound.
Another subject with which I suggest the minister should deal this evening is the recommendation by the commissioners that there should be only one board supervising railways, shipping, and aviation. Their findings on that question will be found at page 276 of the report under the heading "Coordination." They point out that at the present time the board of transport commissioners in reality has jurisdiction only over the railways and certain small portions of the shipping activities of the country. Then there is the air transport board, which has charge of aviation activities, and the Canadian maritime commission, which has most of the authority in connection with shipping in Canada.
Back in 1938, as the minister will remember, a bill was brought into the house and passed entitled "The Transport Act". It was declared to be an act to establish a board of transport commissioners for Canada with authority with respect to transport by railways, ships and aircraft. The new board was in effect simply the board of railway commissioners for Canada under a different name. In 1938 the intention was to put all these three activities under one board, but ever since then the government has followed a different policy. By degrees it has transferred the authority to other boards. For example, in 1944 the air transport board was set up, and against the objections of

quite a few of the members of the house, including myself, that air transport board was given all jurisdiction over aviation; in addition it was set up not as an independent judicial body, such as the board of transport commissioners, but set up directly under a minister, and in effect subject to the orders of the minister. It was really just an administrative branch of a department. We protested bitterly at the time about that set-up. Now the commissioners have recommended that this control be taken away from the air transport board and given to the board of transport commissioners.
Then in 1947 the Canadian maritime commission was set up, and as I said a few moments ago was given jurisdiction over shipping. Now the board recommends that jurisdiction too be placed with the board of transport commissioners. Frankly, I have not been able to convince myself that that is a wise recommendation. It may be. I may change my mind on further study, but I believe that the Canadian maritime commission has a function to fulfil in keeping up the merchant fleet of this country and in making provisions for war vessels to be built; it has a function that can never be adequately fulfilled by the board of transport commissioners. However, such is the recommendation of the Turgeon commission.
Dealing with co-ordination, they say at page 280:
All this leads to the question whether the policy of close co-ordination and central control to which parliament seemed inclined to commit itself in the Transport Act of 1938, should not be invoked once again with the view to its extension rather than to its restriction which has been the trend of more recent enactments. If this policy of 1938 can be revised and made effective it should properly have its beginning in the establishment of a strong control organism capable of taking the task in hand.
They mean by that strengthening of the board of transport commissioners, I presume. Then the paragraph goes on:
Today there are three separate bodies, each charged with the control (a more or less extensive control in each case) of a part of Canada's transportation system. They are the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board and the Canadian maritime commission. It must be difficult, with this dispersion of control, to apply to all of Canada's transportation agencies like principles of regulation for the accomplishment of a common purpose, namely, that of enabling each agency to perform its service advantageously and properly as part of a national transportation structure. The tendency of a separate independent body is to formulate policy affecting transportation without regard to the relationship of the various agencies to each other.
This anomaly-
And here is the recommendation:
-should give way to the constitution of a central authority which will be able to take in hand the major task of co-ordinated control, having at its

disposal all the benefit acquired from the experience of the separate bodies in recent years.
The adoption of this policy would bring together the three above named bodies, reorganized and united and devoted henceforth to the pursuit of a well planned policy for the co-ordination and regulation of transportation.
That is a very definite finding, and I believe the House of Commons should be told what the attitude of the government is with regard to that recommendation.
Another subject dealt with at length by the commission is the refinancing of the Canadian National Railways. As the minister knows, I am no financial wizard; I shall leave that subject to the hon. member for Greenwood. But I believe we should know the attitude of the government toward recommendations made by the commission for the refinancing of the Canadian National Railways.
There is one other recommendation on which I should like to have the government's view, and that has to do with the expansion of railways. The recommendation is found at page 130 of the report, under the heading "Proposed railway expansion and matters incidental thereto." After dealing with the situation in the United States with regard to the expansion of railways, the report states:
In Canada the situation is somewhat different. There is still room for railway expansion where it is called for by the needs of settlers already established in productive areas or by the necessity of making available new areas possessing mineral and other natural resources attainable only by railway.
I point out the words "already established in productive areas." It continues:
It seems to be generally assumed that most, if not all, railway expansion in the foreseeable future will be carried on by the government of Canada or by the Canadian National Railways which the government owns. The day of ill-conceived and therefore excessive construction seems to have gone by, and our people can feel reasonably assured that from now on no railway ventures will be undertaken excepting after thorough investigation of each project and always with due regard to the financial commitments involved.
That sounds like a very reasonable recommendation. No doubt nearly everyone in the chamber this evening has nodded his head, and thought, "That is a good suggestion; that would be a good policy." I am not so sure that in adopting that attitude we are thinking in the year 1951. I am a little afraid that we are looking back to those days thirty years ago when we had a lot of railway trouble, to the days when the Canadian National Railways had to be set up and when everyone became thoroughly hostile to the spending of money for the laying down of further railways.
Supply-Transport
I think the commissioners have been bitten by that bug. I am not so sure that Canada should adopt such a reactionary policy with regard to the building of railways. For example, the commissioners say in this paragraph:
There is still room for railway expansion where it is called for by the needs of settlers already established in productive areas.
It is not so easy to get people to go into those areas when they have no chance of getting railway communication for many years. It just does not work out that way. We have one good example in Canada of the weakness of such a policy, and that is to be found in the Peace river country. There we have a great producing area, the citizens of which are among the outstanding pioneers of our generation. Yet they have never been able to get a railway outlet to the Pacific coast.
Every year since I came here there has been a plea in the house by members from all parties for the building of such a railway, but nothing has been done about it. That railway is no nearer being built today than it was twenty years ago, and if the policy set out at page 130 of the Turgeon commission report is followed in detail by the government there will not be much chance of a rail outlet to the Pacific coast from the Peace river area during the lifetime of the present government. I hope of course that that may not be very long. But, speaking seriously, I think we must be careful not to permit our thinking to get into a groove, and that we must not fail to realize that conditions are changing.
Great developments are going on in Canada today. There are great developments in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, northern Manitoba, northern Saskatchewan, northern Alberta, northern British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and in Labrador. For this country to adopt a policy whereby there would be no railways built until there are plenty of settlers up there who are able to produce, and to fail to supply the only possible way in which they can send out their products, would be unwise. I hope the government will not accede to this recommendation by the-commission.
Those are the only points in the report about which I would ask the minister to make a statement this evening. I regret that the commission failed to deal with the St. Lawrence waterway. I realize it was not instructed to do so, and that it might have been difficult to reach any definite conclusion in the matter. However, if the St. Lawrence seaway is constructed there will be many far-reaching results to the transportation system

Supply-Transport
of Canada, and certainly that of eastern Canada. I regret that no provision has been made for studying the effect on our transportation system of the construction of that seaway. If we had the results of such a study we would be much better able to bring good judgment to bear on the project than we are going to be able to do under present conditions.
